items.title: Trump administration wants to remove regulations on a super planet-heating gas
items.author: Julia Simon
items.summary: The Trump administration is proposing to roll back Biden-era regulations aimed at curbing methane emissions from the oil and gas industry. The move seeks to reduce production costs and encourage domestic drilling, though critics argue it may waste sellable product and hinder leak detection.

also.author: The Editorial Board
also.title: Opinion | Trump Scores on Methane Regulation
also.note: The Wall Street Journal frames the rollback as a political victory for the administration.

also.author: The Editors
also.title: Trump’s Rollback of Methane Regulations Is Welcome
also.note: The National Review frames the deregulation as a positive and welcome development.

brief.what: The Trump administration announced plans to scale back 2023 EPA regulations on methane emissions from oil and gas drilling sites. This includes eliminating the 'Methane Super Emitter Program,' which utilizes third-party monitoring to detect large leaks, and loosening requirements for marginal oil wells.
brief.who: The Trump administration and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin are leading the rollback, supported by the American Petroleum Institute. They are opposed by environmental groups like the Environmental Defense Fund, represented by Jon Goldstein, who argue that capturing methane is economically beneficial.
brief.context: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and the 2023 rules were designed to mitigate its environmental impact. The industry previously opposed these regulations, citing compliance challenges, while the administration claims the revision will lower production costs and boost domestic energy output.
brief.why: President Trump stated the revision would save the industry billions in production costs and spur drilling. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin claimed the previous rules destructively targeted the economy, while industry representatives seek a more 'workable approach' to regulation.
brief.next: The EPA plans to hold a public comment period of at least 45 days, including a public hearing, following the publication of the proposed changes in the Federal Register.

items.title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
items.author: Gaya Gupta
items.summary: The Federal Reserve has maintained current interest rates in its final meeting before the midterm elections, despite inflation remaining above 3%. The decision reflects a wait-and-see approach as officials monitor economic data and global supply shocks.

also.note: Fox Business highlights the political timing of the decision in relation to the upcoming midterms.

brief.what: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at a range of 3.75% to 4% during its final meeting before the midterm elections. While inflation rose to 3.7% in September, the central bank opted for a pause to evaluate incoming economic information.
brief.who: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh led the decision, while board members Christopher Waller and Nicholas Economides provided perspective on policy timing and the limitations of rate hikes against supply-driven inflation.
brief.context: The Fed is balancing its mandate for price stability against inflation driven by global supply shocks, specifically rising oil prices due to the conflict in the Middle East. The decision occurs amid intense political scrutiny regarding the economy's impact on upcoming congressional elections.
brief.why: Chair Warsh stated that politics played no role in the decision, emphasizing that the board is focused on data-driven policy. Experts suggest the pause avoids radical action during an election period where the economy would not have time to adjust to policy shifts.
brief.next: The Fed plans to reduce its annual interest-rate-setting meetings to seven in 2027 and six in 2028, while most economists still anticipate one additional rate hike before the end of the year.

brief.what: Discussions are emerging regarding the necessity of revising rules that govern credit and responsibility for scientific papers produced with the assistance of artificial intelligence.
brief.who: The scientific community is the primary actor involved in evaluating how to attribute authorship for machine-written academic work.
brief.context: As AI tools become more integrated into research workflows, existing academic standards for authorship are being challenged, necessitating a potential reboot of current policies.
brief.why: The debate is driven by the need to establish clear accountability and credit systems for research papers that incorporate machine-generated content.

items.title: Google’s $500bn bloodbath reflects the danger it faces from AI
items.summary: Google is facing significant market pressure as its search engine performance falters and competitors leverage artificial intelligence to gain market share. The company has seen a $500 billion decline in market valuation amid these mounting challenges.

brief.what: Google has experienced a $500 billion loss in market value as its core search engine business faces performance issues and increased competition.
brief.who: Google is the primary company affected by these market shifts.
brief.context: The company is currently navigating a transition where its traditional search engine dominance is being challenged by rivals utilizing artificial intelligence.
brief.why: The article states that Google's search engine is sputtering, allowing competitors to gain ground in the evolving technological landscape.

numbers.what: decline in Google's market valuation

items.title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
items.author: Ollie Lewis for MetDesk
items.summary: Severe weather systems, including heavy rainfall, cyclones, and typhoons, are causing widespread disruption across Europe, Asia, and the Pacific. Authorities have issued flood warnings as regions face significant infrastructure damage and safety risks.

brief.what: Multiple extreme weather events are impacting global regions, including flooding in Greece and Turkey, Cyclone Arnab in India, and Typhoon In-fa in the Pacific. These storms have caused fatalities, mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, and significant damage to energy and transport infrastructure.
brief.who: Authorities in Greece, Turkey, and India are managing emergency responses, while meteorological agencies are tracking the paths of Cyclone Arnab, Typhoon In-fa, and Tropical Storm Vance.
brief.context: The events are driven by various atmospheric phenomena, including low-pressure systems in Europe, a cyclone in the Indian Ocean, and multiple super typhoons in the Pacific, which have already impacted the Mariana Islands this year.
brief.why: The storms are occurring due to the formation of powerful thunderstorms, low-pressure areas, and tropical cyclone development, which have resulted in heavy rainfall, high wind gusts, and dangerous coastal conditions.
brief.next: The systems are expected to continue moving across their respective regions, with some weakening over time while others continue to deliver heavy rain and cause potential landslides.
